lesson.title: Reading a Mass Spectrum: Turning Peaks Into Numbers
lesson.summary: Mass spectrum analysis is the skill of reading a plot of ion abundance against mass-to-charge ratio to identify isotopes and calculate an element's average atomic mass.
lesson.body:
A mass spectrometer produces raw data, but that data only becomes useful once someone reads it correctly. Mass spectrum analysis is the practice of interpreting the graph a mass spectrometer outputs, using the same graph-reading skills used for any scientific plot: identifying what each axis represents, reading peak positions accurately, and comparing peak heights or areas to extract quantitative information. A mass spectrum plots mass-to-charge ratio, usually written m/z, on the horizontal axis, and relative abundance or relative intensity, usually as a percentage, on the vertical axis. Each distinct peak on the graph corresponds to one isotope present in the sample, assuming the ions carry a single positive charge, which is the most common case for elemental analysis.

The first analytical step is reading peak position along the horizontal axis, which tells you the mass number, or very nearly the atomic mass, of the isotope responsible for that peak. The second step is reading peak height along the vertical axis, which tells you that isotope's relative abundance, typically already expressed as a percentage of the total sample. This is exactly the same graph literacy used in any x-y data plot: locate a point, read its coordinates against each axis, and interpret what those coordinates mean physically, here connecting a peak's horizontal position to mass and its vertical position to abundance.

Consider a worked example using magnesium, which has three naturally occurring isotopes. A magnesium mass spectrum shows a tall peak at m/z 24 with a relative abundance of about 78.99 percent, a small peak at m/z 25 with abundance about 10.00 percent, and another small peak at m/z 26 with abundance about 11.01 percent. Reading straight off the graph, without any prior knowledge of magnesium, you can determine that magnesium has three isotopes with mass numbers 24, 25, and 26, and that the lightest isotope, magnesium-24, dominates the natural sample by a wide margin, since its peak towers over the other two.

Once the abundances and masses are read from the graph, calculating average atomic mass follows the same weighted-average method covered earlier. For magnesium: 0.7899 times 23.985 u, plus 0.1000 times 24.986 u, plus 0.1101 times 25.983 u. Computing each term: 0.7899 times 23.985 is about 18.945 u, 0.1000 times 24.986 is about 2.499 u, and 0.1101 times 25.983 is about 2.861 u. Adding these three contributions, 18.945 plus 2.499 plus 2.861, gives about 24.305 u, which matches magnesium's periodic table average atomic mass of 24.305 closely, confirming the graph was read correctly.

Mass spectrum analysis is where mass spectrometry's raw instrument output becomes genuinely useful chemical information, and it depends entirely on careful, accurate graph reading. A common mistake is misreading peak height as an absolute count rather than a relative percentage, or misjudging a peak's exact horizontal position when peaks sit close together. Because the final average atomic mass calculation is only as accurate as the values read from the graph, precise graph-reading technique is not a side skill here, it is the entire method by which real isotope abundance data gets turned into the numbers printed on the periodic table.
